title: SELECT and the WHERE Clause
description: Retrieve exactly the data you need: write SELECT statements, filter rows with WHERE, and combine conditions using AND, OR, BETWEEN, LIKE, and IN.

data.text: The SELECT statement is the workhorse of SQL — it retrieves data from one or more tables. Combined with the WHERE clause, you can pull exactly the rows you need instead of everything.

A basic SELECT has three parts:

1. **SELECT** — which columns you want to see
2. **FROM** — which table to read them from
3. **WHERE** — (optional) conditions that rows must satisfy

data.title: Basic SELECT
data.code:
SELECT first_name, last_name, email
FROM   sales.customers;

data.title: SELECT * vs. explicit columns
data.text: SELECT * grabs every column. It is handy for exploring unfamiliar data, but in production code you should always list the exact columns you need — it is faster and survives column changes to the table.

The WHERE clause keeps only rows where the condition is TRUE. SQL Server uses three-valued logic (TRUE / FALSE / UNKNOWN), and only TRUE rows pass through. This is why = NULL never works — use IS NULL instead.

data.title: Simple equality filter
data.code:
SELECT product_name, list_price
FROM   production.products
WHERE  category_id = 1
ORDER BY list_price DESC;

data.title: AND — both must be true
data.code:
SELECT product_name, list_price
FROM   production.products
WHERE  category_id = 1
   AND model_year = 2018;

data.title: OR — either can be true
AND vs. OR precedence
data.text: AND binds tighter than OR. The condition 'a = 1 OR b = 2 AND c = 3' is parsed as 'a = 1 OR (b = 2 AND c = 3)'. When in doubt, add parentheses to be explicit.

rows: Matches any value in a list

data.title: BETWEEN (inclusive range)
IN (match any value in a list)
LIKE — pattern matching with wildcards
data.content:
%  matches zero or more characters
_  matches exactly one character

data.title: LIKE examples
data.code:
WHERE product_name LIKE '%Cruiser%'   -- contains 'Cruiser'
WHERE product_name LIKE 'Trek%'        -- starts with 'Trek'
WHERE product_name LIKE '_ike%'         -- third char is 'i', then 'ke'

data.title: NOT before the operator
data.text: You can negate any of these: NOT BETWEEN, NOT IN, NOT LIKE. These are especially handy for finding missing data — e.g., WHERE order_id NOT IN (1, 2, 3) finds everything except orders 1, 2, and 3.
Even though SELECT appears first, SQL Server processes clauses in this order:

items: WHERE — keep only rows that match the condition
SELECT — pick and compute the output columns
ORDER BY — sort the final result

data.title: Why the order matters
data.text: Because WHERE runs before SELECT, you cannot filter on a computed alias. Use the full expression instead — e.g., WHERE list_price * 1.1 > 100, not WHERE discounted_price > 100.

data.title: Quick reference
points: SELECT columns FROM table WHERE condition
WHERE only keeps rows where the condition is TRUE
AND means both sides must be true; OR means either side can be true
BETWEEN/IN/LIKE cover most filtering needs — remember BETWEEN is inclusive
Never use = NULL; use IS NULL instead
WHERE runs before SELECT — so you can't reference column aliases in WHERE
